The Romance of Classic Touring

There is something deeply satisfying about touring the UK on a classic motorcycle. The mechanical connection, the absence of electronic nannies, and the character of an older machine create an experience that modern bikes, for all their superiority, cannot replicate. Classic touring is slower, more involving, and arguably more rewarding than riding the latest technology.

What Makes a Good Classic Tourer?

Not all classic bikes are suitable for touring. The ideal classic tourer needs reliability, parts availability, reasonable comfort, and enough performance for modern traffic. Avoid rare exotics where parts require months of searching and choose popular models with strong owner communities.

Best Classic Touring Bikes

BMW R 80 GS / R 100 GS (1980-1996) — The original adventure tourer. Air-cooled boxer twins are simple, reliable, and endlessly repairable. Parts are readily available and the owner community is huge. These bikes were built for touring and remain superb at it. Budget two to six thousand pounds for good examples.

Honda CB750 (1969-1978) — The bike that defined the modern motorcycle. The inline four is smooth and reliable, parts are widely available, and the ride quality is surprisingly good by modern standards. A genuine classic that handles British roads well.

Triumph Bonneville T100 (2001-2016) — Modern classic with genuine retro appeal. The fuel-injected 865cc twin is reliable and economical. It is arguably a modern bike in classic clothing, which makes it perfect for touring — classic style with contemporary dependability.

Yamaha SR500 / XT500 — The big thumper singles are characterful touring companions. Light weight makes them agile on B-roads and the simplicity means roadside repairs are possible with basic tools. Limited luggage capacity but perfect for credit card touring.

Moto Guzzi V7 (2008-present) — Italian character with a transverse V-twin. Shaft drive eliminates chain hassle and the engine has a charismatic rumble. Parts are available through the active Guzzi community.

Classic Touring Preparation

  • Full service — Points, plugs, oil, filters, valve clearances. A well-serviced classic is surprisingly reliable.
  • Electrics — The Achilles heel of classic bikes. Check all connections, replace suspect wiring, and carry spare fuses and bulbs.
  • Tyres — Modern classic-pattern tyres from Avon, Metzeler, and Bridgestone offer period looks with modern grip. Never tour on old, hard tyres.
  • Toolkit — Classic bikes may need roadside attention. Carry a comprehensive toolkit including spanners, screwdrivers, spare cables, and electrical tape.
Classic touring is about the journey, not the speed. Accept that you will ride slower, stop more often, and attract more attention at every cafe stop. That is the charm of it. Embrace the pace and the character.

faq.q: What makes a classic bike suitable for touring?
faq.a: Not all classics tour well. The ideal classic tourer combines reliability, ready parts availability, reasonable comfort and enough performance for modern traffic. Avoid rare exotics where parts take months to find, and choose popular models such as an air-cooled BMW GS or Honda CB750 that have large, active owner communities. A well-supported, thoroughly serviced classic is surprisingly dependable on tour.

faq.q: Are classic bikes reliable enough for a long tour?
faq.a: With proper preparation, yes. A full service covering points, plugs, oil, filters and valve clearances, plus attention to the electrics, transforms reliability. Electrics are the classic bike's Achilles heel, so check all connections, replace suspect wiring and carry spare fuses and bulbs. Fit fresh tyres and pack a comprehensive toolkit, and a well-sorted classic will cover big distances happily.

faq.q: How much should I budget for a classic tourer?
faq.a: It varies widely by model. Good air-cooled BMW GS boxers sit around two to six thousand pounds, while modern classics like the Bonneville T100 or Moto Guzzi V7 command more but offer contemporary reliability. Factor in a thorough pre-tour service, fresh tyres and any electrical work on top of the purchase price. Popular models hold value and are cheaper to maintain than rare machines.

faq.q: What should I check before touring on a classic?
faq.a: Carry out a full service, inspect and refresh the electrics, and fit modern classic-pattern tyres from a brand like Avon or Metzeler for period looks with modern grip. Never tour on old, hard rubber. Pack a comprehensive toolkit including spanners, screwdrivers, spare cables and electrical tape, because a classic may need roadside attention that a modern bike would not.
